456.title: Sleeping tendencies
456.hook: even a baby carries the tendencies to view, doubt and desire, asleep
456.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching the five lower fetters and the underlying tendencies are taught as part of the stages of awakening, and meditators are trained to notice how irritation or desire arise before acting on them.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the undeclared, ten questions the Buddha set aside, and the poisoned arrow. Did one question stay open while you did the next useful thing? Day four hundred fifty-six.
screen: `THE UNDECLARED.`

segments.voice: A baby asleep on its back, arms flung up, completely at peace. No opinions. No grudges. No wanting anything except, eventually, milk. If anyone is free of the troubles of the mind, surely it's this tiny person. The same monk from yesterday, Māluṅkyāputta, shows up again in the very next sutta. The Buddha asks the monks to recite five fetters, five things that bind a person. Māluṅkyāputta recites them perfectly. And the Buddha isn't pleased. He brings up the baby.
screen: `A BABY ASLEEP.` → `NO OPINIONS, NO GRUDGES.` → `FIVE FETTERS, RECITED PERFECTLY.`

segments.voice: The five are the lower fetters, in this sutta's list: the view that there's a fixed self, doubt, clinging to rules and rituals, sensual desire and ill will. Māluṅkyāputta has the list right. What he's missing is how deep it goes. Wanderers of other sects, the Buddha says, could refute you with one simple picture. Look at a young, tender infant lying on its back. It doesn't even have the idea of a self. How could a self-view arise in it? It has no notion of teachings, so how could it doubt them? It has no notion of rules, no notion of pleasures, no notion of other beings to resent. And yet, he says, the underlying tendency to each of these lies within it. The Pali word is anusaya, from a root meaning to lie down along with. It's the thing lying asleep under the surface. That's the turn in this sutta. A fetter isn't only what you're doing right now. You can be calm, kind, unbothered this afternoon, and the tendency to anger is still asleep in you, waiting for the right provocation. Patient all week, and then someone takes the parking spot. The sutta isn't saying babies are bad. It's saying the roots are older than our opinions. Which is why, later in the same sutta, the Buddha describes a practice that goes below the surface: settling the mind deeply and seeing how everything in it changes. A tendency you've watched wake up is one you can begin to know.
screen: `THE FIVE LOWER FETTERS.` · `A TENDER INFANT ON ITS BACK.` · `ANUSAYA: LYING ASLEEP BENEATH.` · `CALM TODAY, STILL THERE.` · then, large: `IT SLEEPS IN US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch one tendency stir. Sit and settle. Bring to mind something small that usually irritates you: a slow line, a certain tone of voice, a notification. Hold the picture just long enough to feel the first flicker, a tightening in the chest or the jaw. That flicker is a tendency waking up. Don't feed it and don't fight it. Just watch it, and watch it settle. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sleeping tendencies. The anusayas: roots of view, doubt, desire and ill will that lie asleep in us, even in a baby, until something wakes them. Today's word.
screen: `SLEEPING TENDENCIES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it sleeps in us. Today, when you feel a flicker of irritation or wanting, say quietly: there it is, waking up. Day four hundred fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 456 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE YOUNG COLT.`

what it means: roots of self-view, doubt, desire and ill will lie asleep in us, even in a baby, until something wakes them.
what a scholar hears: MN 64, the Mahāmāluṅkya Sutta; anusaya, often 'latent tendency', became a major topic in Abhidhamma and in later debates between schools.

457.title: The young colt
457.hook: Bhaddali won't keep the one-meal rule; a good horse is trained step by step
457.howItsDone: Theravada monks and nuns do not eat after midday, and some keep to one meal a day; communities correct members who struggle with a rule; lay Buddhists who keep eight precepts on observance days also skip the evening meal.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sleeping tendencies, the roots that lie asleep in us, even in a baby. Your line was it sleeps in us. Did you catch one tendency waking up? Day four hundred fifty-seven.
screen: `IT SLEEPS IN US.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells the monks he eats once a day, at one sitting, and feels light and healthy for it. He invites them to do the same. One monk, Bhaddāli, says flatly: I can't. I'd worry about it. The Buddha offers a compromise: eat part at the meal, and take the rest to eat later. Bhaddāli says no to that too. And then, for the entire three months of the rains retreat, he avoids the Buddha completely. It's a very human pair: the rule he won't keep, and the teacher he stops looking in the eye.
screen: `ONE MEAL A DAY.` → `I CAN'T.` → `THREE MONTHS OF AVOIDING HIM.`

segments.voice: At the end of the retreat, the monks are sewing a robe for the Buddha before he leaves on his travels, and they tell Bhaddāli: this is your chance. Go and make it right. So he does. He admits he was foolish and wrong. And the Buddha accepts it, but he doesn't rush past it either. He tells Bhaddāli plainly what he'd failed to see: that people had noticed, monks and nuns and lay followers, that he wasn't fulfilling the training. Later Bhaddāli asks a fair question: why are some monks pressed hard over a fault and others left alone? The Buddha's answer: it depends on whether they keep making excuses, or whether they can hear correction. Then the Buddha reminds him of a picture. A skilled horse trainer gets a fine young colt. What does he do first? He gets it used to wearing the bit. And the colt fights it. It twists and resists, because it's never done anything like this before. But with repetition, step by step, it settles. Then the trainer adds the harness. Then keeping in step, running in a circle, galloping, and so on, one stage at a time, until the colt is worthy of a king. That's the training, the Buddha says. Not one leap. A long series of small things, each strange at first. The colt isn't a bad horse for resisting the bit. Resisting is what a colt does on its first day. Repetition, stage by stage, is what settles it. The colt learns, one strange step at a time.
screen: `THE ROBE AND THE APOLOGY.` · `THE COLT FIGHTS THE BIT.` · `THEN THE HARNESS, ONE STAGE AT A TIME.` · `REPETITION SETTLES IT.` · then, large: `THE COLT LEARNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one training. Sit and settle. Think of one small discipline you've been resisting: a bedtime, a budget, a daily walk, something someone wise suggested. Notice the twist in you that says I can't. You don't have to argue with it. Picture the colt with the bit, resisting, and then, a little later, quieter. Choose one small piece of that training to try today, just the bit, not the whole harness. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
The young colt. A good horse is trained step by step, and resists at first, because everything new feels wrong. Today's word.
screen: `THE YOUNG COLT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the colt learns. Today, when a new discipline chafes, let it chafe, and do the small piece anyway. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

screen: `DAY 457 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE QUAIL AND THE CREEPER.`

what it means: a picture of training: the colt fights the bit at first, then learns, stage by stage, until it's worthy of a king.
what a scholar hears: MN 65, the Bhaddāli Sutta; the thoroughbred horse appears elsewhere in the Pali texts too, as a picture of a disciple in training.

458.title: The quail and the creeper
458.hook: a quail held by a rotten creeper, an elephant held by a thick rope: it depends what you believe binds you
458.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics give up eating after midday, and teachers use this sutta to show students that small renunciations are often the hardest, and that letting go of a little thing can loosen a whole habit.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the young colt, who fights the bit at first and learns step by step. Your line was the colt learns. Did you do one small piece of a training that chafed? Day four hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `THE COLT LEARNS.`

segments.voice: A little brown quail is caught in a tangle of rotten vine. One good tug and the vine would snap. But the quail doesn't tug. It sits there, waiting, trapped, until the hunter comes. Now picture a royal elephant, a full-grown tusker, tied with thick leather straps. It shrugs its shoulders, the straps break, and it walks off wherever it likes. Which one is really bound? The sixty-sixth sutta says: that depends less on the rope than you'd think.
screen: `A QUAIL IN A ROTTEN VINE.` → `AN ELEPHANT IN THICK STRAPS.` → `WHICH ONE IS BOUND?`

segments.voice: The sutta starts with a monk named Udāyin, alone, feeling grateful. The Buddha, he remembers, asked the monks to give up eating in the afternoon, and later at night. Some grumbled: must we give up even this little thing? Then Udāyin remembers why it mattered. Monks walking for alms in the pitch dark had stumbled into cesspits and thornbushes. Once, he says, a woman washing a pot saw him by a flash of lightning and screamed that a demon was after her. He's glad now. The Buddha answers with the quail. Some people, told to give up some small thing, say: what, this trifle? And they resent it. For them, he says, that small thing is a strong, thick, tough bond, the way the rotten creeper is for the quail. Others give up the small thing easily, and for them even a thick rope is weak. Then he brings it home. A poor man with a leaking hut, a single bad bed, a pot of rice, can't bring himself to give any of it up. A rich householder with stores of gold might walk away from all of it. The size of the thing isn't the point. What binds is the holding on. On an ordinary day this is everywhere. The one more episode at midnight. The phone you check without wanting to. The argument you can't drop, though you've forgotten what it's about. Each one is a rotten creeper. It looks like a rope because we've never pulled. And the sutta is honest: the creeper doesn't snap by itself. Somebody has to pull. The good news is it's only a creeper.
screen: `UDĀYIN REMEMBERS THE DARK.` · `WHAT, THIS TRIFLE?` · `THE POOR HUT, THE RICH HOUSE.` · `WHAT BINDS IS THE HOLDING ON.` · then, large: `IT'S ONLY A CREEPER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cut one thin creeper. Sit and settle. Let one small habit come to mind, something you keep doing that you'd rather not: a snack, a scroll, a sharp reply. Picture it as a thin, dry vine wrapped around you. Feel how much it seems to hold. Now, on an out-breath, picture yourself simply standing up, and the vine snapping. Decide on one moment today when you'll pull. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The quail and the creeper. A rotten vine holds the quail because it never pulls; thick straps can't hold the elephant. What binds is the holding on. Today's word.
screen: `THE QUAIL AND THE CREEPER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it's only a creeper. Today, when a small habit tugs at you, say the line, and pull once. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

screen: `DAY 458 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOUR DANGERS FOR A SWIMMER.`

what a scholar hears: MN 66, the Laṭukikopama Sutta, set against the background of the rules against eating after midday and at night.

459.title: Four dangers for a swimmer
459.hook: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks: the dangers for someone new to the path
459.howItsDone: Some monastic teachers use this sutta with new monks and nuns, so that the frustration of being corrected or the pull of food and pleasure can be recognized as a stage of training, not a reason to leave.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quail and the creeper. A rotten vine holds the quail only because it never pulls. Your line was it's only a creeper. Did you pull once? Day four hundred fifty-nine.
screen: `IT'S ONLY A CREEPER.`

segments.voice: About five hundred monks arrive at a village called Cātumā with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, some of them newly ordained, and they're loud. Greeting the resident monks, finding beds, arranging bowls and robes, all at once. The Buddha hears the noise, asks what it is, and sends them all away. The local people and, the sutta says, a god named Brahmā Sahampati plead for them: they're new, they're like young seedlings that need water. The Buddha relents. And then, with the new ones sitting in front of him, he tells them what tends to drown beginners.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED MONKS, AND NOISE.` → `SENT AWAY.` → `LIKE SEEDLINGS THAT NEED WATER.`

segments.voice: Someone wading into a river, the sutta says, can expect four dangers: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks. The Buddha names each one for a person who has just entered the training. The waves are anger and frustration at being taught. Do this, don't do that, look ahead, look behind, wear your robe this way. Someone who was used to giving instructions at home now has to take them from people younger than they are, and it stings. A person like this, the sutta says, can give up the training right there. The crocodiles are the stomach. Eat this, don't eat that, not now. The whirlpools are the five kinds of sensual pleasure: what's lovely to see, hear, smell, taste and touch, swirling around a new monk when he walks into the village. The fourth, the sharks, is sexual desire. The text, spoken to monks, names it through women; read today, it's the pull of attraction for anyone in training who has vowed celibacy. None of the four is deep philosophy. In the sutta, what sends a beginner home is being corrected. It's food. It's the scroll of things to want. It's attraction. Knowing which water you're in doesn't make the crocodile go away. But a swimmer who knows the river is less likely to be surprised. And a beginner who's been told the waves will come might feel them and think, ah, this is the wave they meant, instead of, this proves I don't belong here.
screen: `WAVES: ANGER AT BEING TAUGHT.` · `CROCODILES: THE STOMACH.` · `WHIRLPOOLS: THE FIVE PLEASURES.` · `SHARKS: SEXUAL DESIRE.` · then, large: `KNOW THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your four dangers. Sit and settle. Think of something you've started recently and want to keep: a practice, a job, a way of living. Ask, gently: what are my waves, the corrections that sting? My crocodile, the appetite? My whirlpool, the thing that pulls me off? My shark? Give each one a short name, silently. Then let the names go and rest with the breath, like floating. The bell holds the time.
Four dangers for a swimmer. Waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks: anger at being taught, the stomach, the five pleasures, and desire. Today's word.
screen: `FOUR DANGERS FOR A SWIMMER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: know the water. Today, when one of your four shows up, name it: a wave, a crocodile, a whirlpool. Name it, and keep swimming. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 459 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY HE SPEAKS OF REBIRTH.`

460.title: Why he speaks of rebirth
460.hook: the Buddha tells where the dead were reborn to inspire, not to boast
460.howItsDone: Buddhist communities remember teachers and relatives who have died at memorial ceremonies and anniversaries, where people may recall their virtues, offer food to monks, and dedicate merit to them.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: four dangers for a swimmer, waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks. Your line was know the water. Which one did you name when it showed up? Day four hundred sixty.
screen: `KNOW THE WATER.`

segments.voice: At a memorial, someone stands up and tells a story about the person who died. Not their résumé. A small thing. How she always left the last piece of cake for someone else. How he answered every phone call from his brother, even at 3am. And people in the room quietly decide to be a bit more like that. In the sixty-eighth sutta, at a grove called Naḷakapāna, the Buddha explains why he talks about monks and nuns and lay followers who have died, and where they went. It turns out to be the same reason.
screen: `A STORY AT A MEMORIAL.` → `THE LAST PIECE OF CAKE.` → `THE SAME REASON.`

segments.voice: He starts by asking a group of young men who had left home together, Anuruddha among them, whether they're happy in the holy life. They say yes. Then he raises a question someone might fairly ask. When a disciple dies, the Buddha sometimes tells people where that person was reborn, or that they reached final freedom. Isn't that a little like boasting? Isn't it a show? He answers directly. He doesn't do it to deceive people, or to flatter them, or for gain, or honor, or fame, or so that people will think, what a teacher. He does it for one reason: for people of faith who will hear it and be inspired. Then he describes how that works. A monk hears that a certain elder has died, and that the Buddha said he reached freedom. And he thinks: I saw that elder myself, or I've heard about him. His conduct was like this, his calm was like this, his understanding was like this. And the monk turns his own mind toward that. The sutta repeats it for nuns, for laymen, and for laywomen. Each hears of someone like themselves who went before, and directs their mind to the same goodness. The sutta doesn't explain here how rebirth works. What it explains is the purpose of telling. A life well lived, spoken about honestly after it ends, becomes a path someone else can see. The story isn't for the dead. It's for the ones still walking.
screen: `ARE YOU HAPPY HERE? YES.` · `NOT TO BOAST, NOT FOR FAME.` · `I KNEW THAT ELDER.` · `MONKS, NUNS, LAYMEN, LAYWOMEN.` · then, large: `TO INSPIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone who went before. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone who has died, whose way of living you admired: a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor. Picture one concrete thing they did, the way they spoke or gave or listened. Let yourself be glad they lived. Then turn your mind toward that one quality, the way the monk in the sutta does, and quietly let it become yours for today. The bell holds the time.
Why he speaks of rebirth. Not to boast, not for fame, but so those still on the path can hear of someone who went before and be inspired. Today's word.
screen: `WHY HE SPEAKS OF REBIRTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: to inspire. Today, tell someone one good thing about a person who has died, a small, true thing they did. Day four hundred sixty.

461.title: Coming back well
461.hook: a forest monk who returns to the community should come back with respect
461.howItsDone: In Theravada forest lineages, monks may spend stretches in solitude and then return to the monastery for communal occasions, where seating follows seniority and courtesy to fellow monastics is expected.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: why he speaks of rebirth. Not to boast, but so the living can be inspired. Your line was to inspire. Whose small, true goodness did you pass on? Day four hundred sixty-one.
screen: `TO INSPIRE.`

segments.voice: You've been away. Six months working remotely, a semester abroad, a long stretch of caring for a parent in another city. Now you're walking back into the office, the class, the family dinner. Everyone has moved on a bit. There are new jokes you don't get. And there's a temptation, quietly, to come back as the one who's been somewhere. A monk named Gulissāni lived in the forest, alone. One day he comes into the monastery on some business. And Sāriputta takes the opportunity to give a talk about how to come back.
screen: `YOU'VE BEEN AWAY.` → `NEW JOKES YOU DON'T GET.` → `GULISSĀNI COMES IN FROM THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Sāriputta doesn't scold Gulissāni. He speaks to the room. A forest monk who comes back to the community, he says, should be respectful and deferential toward his companions. If he isn't, people will say: what good is all his solitude, if he can't even treat his fellow monks with respect? Then come the details, and they're wonderfully ordinary. Be skilled about where you sit. Don't push in on the elders, and don't push the younger monks off their seats. Don't go into the village too early, or come back too late. Don't drop in on families before or after the meal. Don't be restless or fidgety. Don't chatter. Be easy to correct. Guard your senses, eat in moderation, stay awake and mindful. And knowing the teaching matters too: people will ask the forest monk about it. Every item ends the same way. If he doesn't do this, there'll be some who say: what's the use of his forest life? Then Moggallāna asks a good question. Is this only for forest monks? No, says Sāriputta. It's even more so for those who live near a village. The point isn't that solitude is suspect; nothing in the sutta speaks against the forest. The point is that solitude is tested in company. Whatever you gained alone shows up in where you sit, when you arrive, and how well you take correction. Coming back well isn't a performance of humility. It's where the time away shows.
screen: `SPEAKING TO THE ROOM.` · `WHERE YOU SIT, WHEN YOU ARRIVE.` · `EASY TO CORRECT.` · `VILLAGE MONKS TOO.` · then, large: `COME BACK WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoin one group well. Sit and settle. Think of a group you'll walk back into soon, a team, a class, a family table, a friend circle you've drifted from. Picture arriving. Where will you sit? Who might you listen to first, instead of telling your news? Who's younger, or newer, that you could make room for? Let the picture be small and practical. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Coming back well. Sāriputta's advice to a forest monk returning to the community: respect, good timing, easy to correct. Solitude tested in company. Today's word.
screen: `COMING BACK WELL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: come back well. Today, when you rejoin any group, arrive on time, listen first, and make room for someone newer. Day four hundred sixty-one.

462.title: Step by step
462.hook: final knowledge is not reached all at once but by gradual training
462.howItsDone: Lay Buddhist practice can follow this sutta's order: visiting a temple, teacher or group, listening to talks, keeping simple precepts, and deepening over years.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: coming back well, Sāriputta's advice to the forest monk. Your line was come back well. Did you listen first when you rejoined a group? Day four hundred sixty-two, the end of a week.
screen: `COME BACK WELL.`

segments.voice: Nobody reads their first page of music and plays a concerto. Nobody wakes up fluent. It's tempting to hope the inner life works differently: one retreat, one book, one night under the stars, and then everything is different. The seventieth sutta begins with two monks at a place called Kīṭāgiri who refuse the Buddha's advice about meals. It's Bhaddāli's story again, from five days ago, with new names. But this time the Buddha uses the occasion to say something larger, about how anyone arrives at all.
screen: `NOBODY WAKES UP FLUENT.` → `TWO MONKS AT KĪṬĀGIRI.` → `HOW ANYONE ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: I do not say, the Buddha tells the monks, that final knowledge is reached all at once. It's reached by gradual training, gradual practice, gradual progress. Then he lays out the steps, and they're surprisingly human. Someone has some faith, enough to go and visit a teacher. Having visited, they sit near. Sitting near, they listen. Listening, they hear the teaching. Then they remember it. Then they examine what it means. Examining, they come to accept it, not blindly, but after looking. From acceptance, enthusiasm. From enthusiasm, they make an effort. With effort, they weigh things up. Weighing, they strive. And striving, they see the truth for themselves. A dozen steps, and the first is just turning up. Look at what that means for the rest of us. The person who went to a meditation group once and sat at the back has already taken the first three steps. The person who remembered one line from a talk is on step six. Nobody is asked to leap to the end. Of the two monks who wouldn't listen, the Buddha says only this: how far they have strayed from the teaching. The Dhammapada has a picture for gradual work. In Max Müller's words: "Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time." Little by little isn't a lesser path. In this sutta, it's the path itself.
screen: `NOT ALL AT ONCE.` · `FAITH, VISIT, SIT NEAR, LISTEN.` · `REMEMBER, EXAMINE, ACCEPT, STRIVE.` · `THE SMITH AND THE SILVER.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step. Sit and settle. Think of the path you're on, any path, and ask honestly: which step am I on? Turning up? Listening? Remembering? Testing what I've heard? Don't judge the answer. Then name the very next step, just one. Picture yourself taking it today. Let the breath be slow, one breath after another, the same way. The bell holds the time.
Step by step. Final knowledge isn't reached all at once, the Buddha says, but by gradual training, from simply turning up to seeing for yourself. Today's word.
screen: `STEP BY STEP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: step by step. Take one step today. And that's week sixty-six: sleeping tendencies, the young colt, the quail, four dangers, why he speaks of rebirth, coming back well, and step by step. Day four hundred sixty-two.
screen: `WEEK SIXTY-SIX: TENDENCIES · COLT · QUAIL · FOUR DANGERS · REBIRTH · COMING BACK · STEP BY STEP`

original.note: Pali anupubba: gradual, in due order. the sutta speaks of gradual training, practice and progress.

trapdoor: what you thought: step by step means slowly.
what it means: awakening comes through a sequence, from faith and listening to seeing for yourself, with no step skipped.
what a scholar hears: MN 70, the Kīṭāgiri Sutta, also gives a list of seven kinds of noble person, and its gradual sequence is a classic text on how faith and wisdom relate.
